items.title: Simple beats theoretical
items.text: Choose openings built on sound principles rather than endless variations. You leave the opening with confidence and without memory slips.
items.note: Fine advice for club players. At master level theory matters more.

items.title: A doubled pawn is not always weak
items.text: It becomes a problem when it is isolated and cannot be defended. If it takes squares from the opponent and controls the centre, it can be very useful.
items.note: Checked: the weakness usually comes from isolation, blocked pawns or lost flexibility, not from the doubling itself.

items.title: Be flexible in the opening
items.text: You do not have to follow the main line to get a good position. A less common move order makes your opponent think for themselves from the start.
items.note: Checked: works only if you understand the position. Sound principles still come first.

items.title: The three opening principles
items.text: Control the centre, develop your minor pieces and get your king safe. That is what the opening is for. It saves you from aimless moves.
items.note: Checked: the core of the opening. The same list also says: do not move the same piece twice and do not attack too early.

items.title: Be economical with your moves
items.text: Make every move the most active option and skip useless manoeuvres. Lost time in the opening hands your opponent a lead in development.
items.note: Checked: this is the idea of tempo.

items.title: Castle early
items.text: Do not play recklessly: get your king safe early in the opening by castling, before the middlegame breaks loose.
items.note: Checked: standard and sound.

items.title: Flexible move order: centre and development first
items.text: Do not rush to finish a fixed pawn set-up, such as a pawn triangle. First control the centre and develop your minor pieces. The pawn structure can wait.
items.note: Checked: sound, and it fits the opening principles above.

items.title: Pawn support frees your pieces
items.text: A solid pawn defence, such as c6 backing d5, takes defending jobs off your pieces. Once a centre pawn is covered by a pawn, the knight next to it is free to go on the attack.
items.note: Checked: the idea behind the Caro-Kann and Slav set-ups.

items.title: Do not bring the queen out too early
items.text: Do not rush the queen to the centre where enemy minor pieces can attack it. You lose tempo moving it again and again.
items.note: Checked: correct for the opening. A queen move can be fine when nothing can hit it.

items.title: Watch for flank pawns challenging your centre
items.text: Be alert when your opponent tries to trade off your centre pawn with a flank pawn (such as ...c5) and claim the centre. Keep the option of recapturing with a centre pawn of your own.
items.note: Checked: a typical theme (Sicilian, Benoni structures).

items.title: The accordion pawn structure
items.text: In a solid pawn triangle you can sometimes sacrifice or trade a flank pawn and then answer with b4, so that all your pawns link up and cannot be broken.
items.note: Draft: I could not confirm the name "accordion" or this exact idea. It needs a concrete position from Peter before we publish it.

items.title: Attack weak, misplaced pieces at once
items.text: Spot an opponent's misplaced piece, such as a knight on c6 played too early, and put maximum pressure on it with active pieces, for example a bishop on b5 and a queen on a4.
items.note: Checked: sound. Check that the attack does not leave your own pieces loose.

items.title: Build a system opening
items.text: Use a fixed set-up that lets you play the same solid plan against almost any reply, so you have less theory to remember.
items.note: Checked: a real approach (the Colle, London or similar systems). The label 'peer-to-peer recognition' in the notes looks like a dictation error, so I used 'system opening'. The price is less flexibility against well-prepared opponents.

items.title: Use a flexible knight move to prepare e4
items.text: Playing the knight to d2 instead of c3 prepares the strong central break e4, which forces your opponent to answer with a specific move such as ...d5.
items.note: Checked for d4 + e3 set-ups. Softened: it does not force one reply, but ...d5 is the natural one.

items.title: Support your centre pawn, then challenge
items.text: Support your centre pawn with a pawn and a piece, then build up with c4.
items.note: Wording in the source was unclear (which pawn is doubly defended). Kept as a draft until we confirm the position with Peter.

items.title: Queen to b3 at the right moment
items.text: In this type of opening, an early queen move to b3 puts pressure on the undefended b7 pawn, adds force in the centre and helps your bishop development.
items.note: Checked: a known idea. Softened: only when b7 is really loose and the queen cannot be harassed (for example by ...Nxd4 or ...Qb6 tricks). The queen-out-too-early rule still applies.

items.title: Hunt the defending bishop
items.text: If your opponent puts a bishop on f5 or g4 to stop your e4 break, force a trade or chase it with a knight move to h4 to weaken their defence.
items.note: Checked: a typical plan in e3 set-ups. Check that your knight on h4 is not trapped.

items.title: Bring the queen to the centre
items.text: Once the enemy bishop is off the diagonal, you can move the queen (often after a trade) to the centre to control e4 and raise the pressure.
items.note: Checked: sound. Do not leave the queen loose.

items.title: Punish a forced short castle
items.text: If your opponent has to castle short while your pieces and pawns already point at the kingside, destructive sacrifices can be waiting, such as a bishop sacrifice on h6.
items.note: Draft: the classic sacrifice is Bxh7+ (the Greek gift). I could not confirm Bxh6 as a standard idea. Needs a concrete position and a calculation before publishing.

items.title: Punish passive play with a direct break
items.text: If your opponent plays passively, punish it at once by opening the centre with e4, or by letting a knight jump in for a fork.
items.note: Checked: sound. Make sure the break is prepared.

items.title: Create deadly forks in the middlegame
items.text: Keep a sharp eye for tactical moments where a centralized knight or an active queen attacks a king position and pieces at the same time.
items.note: Checked: forks are a main tactic. Use CCTO to find them.

items.title: Keep looking at 'poisoned' pawns
items.text: If your opponent leaves a pawn undefended or open to capture, check whether it is poisoned by a pin or a mate threat before you take it. Punish them with the material loss if it is.
items.note: Checked: always check before taking a free pawn (the same idea as the Fishing Pole Trap).

items.title: Pick a middlegame plan
items.text: After the opening, choose one clear aim, such as a specific pawn break. A plan gives direction to every following move and puts the opponent under pressure.

items.title: Prepare the break, then play it
items.text: Play a thematic pawn break once your pieces stand well to support it. Breaking too early loses pawns; patient preparation slowly squeezes the opponent.
items.note: Checked: a good rule of thumb, not an absolute one. With the initiative, an early break can be right.

items.title: Block the line instead of adding a defender
items.text: A pawn under attack does not always need another defender. Sometimes you can cut the attacking line. That keeps your pieces active instead of passive.

items.title: Simple, controlled play wins
items.text: Choose a simple, controlled style. Winning a single pawn is often enough. Sacrificing pieces without calculating usually just loses material.
items.note: Checked: sound for club play. One pawn is enough only if you convert carefully.

items.title: Optimize: improve your worst piece
items.text: When there is no check, capture or forcing threat, improve your passive pieces, starting with the ones still on your back rank (minor pieces first).
items.note: Checked: this is the 'improve your worst piece' rule.

items.title: Improve with a purpose
items.text: When you reposition a piece such as your queen, prefer an active square that attacks a target (an undefended piece or a pawn) over a passive retreat.
items.note: Checked: sound. Do not leave a piece hanging for the sake of an active square.

items.title: Attack the backward pawn
items.text: A pawn that cannot be supported by other pawns and cannot advance is a weakness. Pile your pressure on it and try to win it step by step.
items.note: Corrected: it is a target, not literally a 'dead pawn'. You will not always win it, but it ties down your opponent's pieces.

items.title: Build up pressure, then break
items.text: When your opponent's pieces are all tied to defending one weakness, create the breaking move (such as an advancing pawn) to open the position. The defence often cracks.
items.note: Softened: 'often cracks', not always.

items.title: Pawns leave holes behind
items.text: A pawn that moves forward can never protect the square it left. When pawns advance too far, holes appear where the opponent can plant a piece for good.
items.note: Checked: true. Softened: a hole only hurts if an enemy piece can actually use it.

items.title: Prophylaxis: control the key squares
items.text: Cut off the opponent's counterplay by controlling the key invasion squares before they get there. A key square held in advance leaves them with nothing to do.
items.note: Checked: a classic idea (prophylaxis). It does not make the opponent helpless. Ask yourself every move: which checks, captures or threats can my opponent play? If needed, play a prophylactic move before it gets painful.

items.title: After you win material, check their compensation
items.text: Ask what the opponent got in return, for example the bishop pair. Then trade off that specific advantage.
items.note: Checked: good habit. Material is not everything, so look at what the other side gained.

items.title: Optimize with a pawn move (gain space)
items.text: A pawn move can also be an improving move, if it seriously restricts the opponent's pieces or takes extra space, for example ...c6 against the opponent's pieces.
items.note: Checked: a good idea. Check the weaknesses the pawn move leaves behind.

items.title: Activate a passive piece in time
items.text: If one of your pieces, such as a rook, has stood passively on the back rank through the whole middlegame, look for a moment to activate it for a break or to pressure the enemy weaknesses.
items.note: Checked: this is the "improve your worst piece" idea for the rook.

items.title: A fixed thinking system: CCTO
items.text: Run the same steps every move: Checks, Captures, Threats, then Optimize. It prevents blunders, stops you missing chances and gives consistently good moves. Use it for your opponent too: what checks, captures and threats can they play?
items.note: Checked: CCT is a standard method. The extra O (Optimize) is our coach's addition and is explained next under Middlegame plan.

items.title: Checks, captures, threats (CCT)
items.text: Look for the best move in a structured way: checks, captures and threats, for you and for your opponent. Doing this every move finds tactics that are really there and avoids blunders.
items.note: Checked: a standard thinking method taught by many coaches. It helps you find tactics, it does not guarantee winning material.

items.title: Spot the Fishing Pole Trap pattern
items.text: Do not just grab a 'free' piece when the opponent pushes a rook pawn to open a file towards your king. An offer like this opens attack lines, and your position can collapse in a few moves.
items.note: Example: in our Fishing Pole Trap (Ruy Lopez, Black sets it) the bait is a knight on g4 and Black opens the h-file against the castled king.

items.title: Deal with infiltrators on your half
items.text: Do not leave enemy pieces on your side of the board alone. Trade or chase them early, otherwise they become the base for dangerous combinations against your king.
items.note: Softened: act on it quickly, but only when trading or chasing does not cost you more.

items.title: Back-rank safety
items.text: Watch for mate threats on the back rank, for you and for your opponent. Make a flight square (luft) for your king in time.
items.note: Also in the endgame: when you trade or sacrifice pieces, check the back rank first and adjust your defence in time.

items.title: Master both kinds of blunders
items.text: Avoid giving away your own material (or walking into mate), and avoid missing the chances your opponent offers you. Both kinds of carelessness cost you the game.
items.note: Checked: both matter. One is a mistake you make, the other is a chance you miss.

items.title: Sit on your hands
items.text: Stop at every move of your opponent. Ask: what is the purpose of this move, what would he do with a free move, and does he have checks or captures?
items.note: Checked: a good habit. It is the same question as "what does this move threaten?"

items.title: Solve immediate problems first
items.text: When your opponent creates a threat, such as an attack on a piece or a mate threat, solving it comes before your own attack plan.
items.note: Checked: correct, with one exception: a stronger forcing move of your own (a check or a mate) can come first if you have calculated it.

items.title: Set a trap with a defensive move
items.text: Sometimes a defensive or passive-looking move (such as moving a rook) is a clever trap. The opponent is punished when he tries to grab your poisoned pawn.
items.note: Checked: traps work well at club level. Only set one when your move is also fine if he does not fall for it.

items.title: Play actively and take the initiative
items.text: Take the initiative, put your pieces on their best squares, dominate the centre and claim space, without becoming reckless.
items.note: A style, not a rule. Keep calculating: the other principles still apply. Wanting activity is not an excuse to be reckless.

items.title: Play forcing, active moves in the opening
items.text: Choose opening moves that develop a minor piece and force an active answer, instead of slow, waiting moves.
items.note: Checked: good, as long as the move is also sound.

items.title: Do not defend passively out of fear
items.text: Do not answer what your opponent might do with waiting moves, such as needless edge pawn moves. Carry on with your own plan.
items.note: Checked: but first check the opponent's real threats (see CCTO).

items.title: Build a lead in development
items.text: Bring your minor pieces and queen to their best squares quickly, so you soon lead in development against a slow opponent.
items.note: Checked: standard. A queen that comes out early can still lose tempo.

items.title: Castle long only when it is safe
items.text: Long castling is the most aggressive form, but only castle long when the position allows it and your king is really safe there.
items.note: Checked: correct. The king is a bit more exposed on the queenside and the pawn cover is thinner.

items.title: Keep fighting for the centre
items.text: Let every move contribute to control of the four central squares, by aiming pieces at them or advancing centre pawns.
items.note: Checked: standard.

items.title: Do not react to non-forcing moves
items.text: If your opponent makes a move without a direct threat, do not react straight away. Carry on with your own active plan.
items.note: Softened: first check what the move threatens (not just mate or queen loss, also any piece or pawn). If there is none, ignore it. This does not contradict 'answer the threat first'. Another lesson adds a test: ask "do I lose a piece or the game right now?" Softened: first make sure the move does not create a slower, positional threat.

items.title: Defend aggressively
items.text: When you have to defend, for example against an attack on your queen, try to answer with an attack of your own on an enemy pawn or piece.
items.note: Checked: a good counterpunch, as long as your counter is real.

items.title: Calculate sacrifices three moves deep
items.text: Before you sacrifice a piece, force yourself to calculate at least three moves. If you have not gained anything by then, the sacrifice is probably wrong or too complex.

items.title: Open the king with a pawn storm
items.text: Advance your pawns (such as the g and h pawns) against the enemy king to open lines and files for your rooks.
items.note: Checked: mainly with opposite-side castling. On the same side it loosens your own king.

items.title: Fix problems with pieces, not pawns
items.text: When your king or position is under pressure, solve it by moving a piece rather than pushing a pawn. Pawn moves create permanent weaknesses ('hook pawns').
items.note: Checked: a good default. A pawn move is sometimes right, for example to make luft.

items.title: Do not panic and weaken
items.text: When your opponent attacks, do not weaken your own pawn structure. Keep your attacking tempo and keep pushing forward.
items.note: Checked: keep calm; only keep pushing when your own attack is real.

items.title: Force reactions with early threats
items.text: Play so your opponent has to answer your threats all the time. Then he has no time for his own plans.
items.note: Checked: keeping the initiative works, as long as your threats are real.

items.title: Avoid hope chess
items.text: Do not play a move hoping your opponent blunders (such as leaving a bishop hanging). Play on objective pressure and concrete calculation.
items.note: Checked: "hope chess" is a known term. A trap is fine when your move is also sound if he does not fall for it (see "Set a trap with a defensive move").

items.title: Opposite-side castling is a race
items.text: When the kings castle on opposite sides, speed and mating attacks matter most. The player who starts a pawn storm first, with enough pieces behind it, usually gets the better of it.
items.note: Softened: the first version said the first storm almost always wins. Tempo is key, but development and counterplay in the centre still matter.

items.title: Support the pawn storm
items.text: A pawn storm on the wing works best when the leading pawn is supported by another pawn or piece. Support costs less time than waiting for the opponent to regroup.
items.note: Checked: a pawn storm needs a supported spearhead, so the leading pawn is backed by a second pawn or a piece.

items.title: Answer a wing attack in the centre
items.text: If a faster pawn storm hits one wing, look for counterplay by opening the centre. This often changes the course of the game and defuses the wing attack.
items.note: Checked: a classical principle.

items.title: Open lines by trading pawns
items.text: A pawn storm aims to open lines for your rooks and queen by trading pawns. Removing the pawns around the enemy king exposes the defence and makes quick mating patterns possible.
items.note: Checked: correct.

items.title: Prepare the pawn storm
items.text: Do not push a pawn when the opponent can place a blocking knight in front of it and slow you down. Check that knight's landing square before you move the pawn mass forward.
items.note: Checked: correct.

items.title: Exchange sacrifice on the wing
items.text: A rook sacrifice against a defending wing pawn can break open the enemy king position and give your other pieces ways in.
items.note: Softened: only when you can calculate it. The original called it forcing, which is not true in general. This also goes against 'simple, controlled play', so use it only with a clear calculation.

items.title: Trade pieces when ahead
items.text: With a material lead, trading pieces is the fastest way to win. Fewer pieces make it easier to cash in. Trade pieces, not pawns.
items.note: Checked: correct. Be careful with fortress positions. Other lessons say the same: fewer pieces make your extra material weigh more. Another lesson adds: do it once your opponent's attack is neutralized. Softened: it is not completely risk-free. One pawn up is enough to simplify, but see the opposite-coloured bishops warning.

items.title: Create a passed pawn
items.text: Use a majority on one wing to make a pawn that can run to the other side. A passed pawn ties down the opponent and often decides the endgame.

items.title: Rook versus minor piece: win it with technique
items.text: Being up the exchange is a real edge, worth about 1.5 to 2 pawns. Build calmly, activate your king and use the rook to pick up pawns.
items.note: Corrected: it is not automatically won. In the middlegame it usually wins with a pawn or more; in endgames with blocked pawns or no pawns the minor piece can draw.

items.title: Activate your king in the endgame
items.text: In the endgame the king is a strong piece, not a target. Bring it to the centre to support your pawns and block the opponent.
items.note: Checked: true once queens are off and there is no mating danger. Another lesson adds: a central king supports your passed pawns and cuts off the enemy king. Another lesson says the same: once the queens are gone, march the king to the centre.

items.title: Push your passed pawn (PPP)
items.text: If you have a pawn that can promote, support it and push it towards the other side to decide the game.
items.note: Checked: a standard rule. Do not run it unsupported and watch for the enemy king. Priority number one in an endgame when it can run unhindered: push it, but in a controlled way.

items.title: Put your pawns on the opposite colour of the enemy bishop
items.text: If the opponent has a bishop in the endgame, put your pawns and pieces on the other colour (dark squares if his bishop runs on light). The bishop then has nothing to attack.
items.note: Corrected: the title said 'same colour', but the rule is the opposite colour of his bishop. It makes the bishop much weaker, not completely useless.

items.title: Mate with king and queen
items.text: Shrink the box around the enemy king with your queen a knight's move away, bring your own king up, and finish with the 'kiss of death' or a corner mate. Check for stalemate on every move.
items.note: Checked: always wins if you avoid stalemate. Wording: 'mirroring' became 'a knight's move away'.

items.title: Trade queens when you are a pawn up
items.text: With a pawn extra, trading queens is often a good way to simplify and make a setback unlikely.
items.note: Softened: often right, not always. A queenless endgame can still be drawn, and check the trade does not give the opponent compensation.

items.title: Pieces first, then pawns
items.text: In the endgame, activate your pieces and king before you push your pawns.
items.note: Softened: usually. In pawn races, speed can matter more.

items.title: Fewer pawn islands
items.text: Fewer pawn islands are easier to defend. Keep your pawns connected.
items.note: Corrected: the idea is right. The exact rule depends on the position: recapture with the pawn or the piece that keeps your pawns together, not always with a piece.

items.title: Beware opposite-coloured bishops
items.text: Be careful trading into an endgame with opposite-coloured bishops when you are only one pawn up. The defender can often draw easily.
items.note: Checked: correct. With queens and rooks on the board, opposite bishops can help the attacker instead.

items.title: Castling is not automatic without queens
items.text: When queens are off, your king is in less danger. Do not castle out of habit: use the king in the centre to fight and support pawns.
items.note: Checked: castling is just no longer a priority. Also: a short-castled king in the corner can get boxed in and loses tempi getting to the centre. Softened from "almost never": it is just rarely worth the time.

items.title: Doubled isolated pawns are a target
items.text: Aim for positions where the opponent gets doubled, isolated pawns. They are hard to defend and easy to attack in the endgame.
items.note: Checked and aligned with the doubled-pawn principle above: it is the isolation and blocking that make them weak.

items.title: Shelter your king from checks
items.text: In rook endings, put your king behind your own pawns so the enemy rook cannot keep giving checks.
items.note: Checked: a known technique. Balance it with an active king when there are no annoying checks. In won rook endings you can hide king and rook behind or between your own pawns, so that the enemy rook cannot give permanent checks.

items.title: Watch out for stalemate
items.text: When your pawn is about to promote and the enemy king is boxed in, make sure your opponent still has a legal move.
items.note: Checked: stalemate turns wins into draws. In won endgames stay alert until the last move so you do not take away all legal moves before you give mate.

items.title: Stay careful until the last move
items.text: Even in a won endgame one slip can throw away the win or allow a draw. Keep calculating and look for the cleanest forced finish.

items.title: The scissor technique with a bishop
items.text: In the endgame one bishop can sometimes control two enemy passed pawns at once by standing on the right diagonal, as long as you calculate precisely.
items.note: Draft: I could not confirm the name. The idea only works in specific positions. It needs a concrete example before it gets its own page.

items.title: March a pawn majority
items.text: With a pawn majority on the queenside (4 against 2, for example), use it to advance your pawns step by step into a passed pawn and force your opponent into passive defence.
items.note: Checked: a standard endgame plan. Keep the pawns supported and watch the enemy king.
